subtitle: Second benchmark. The schema grew from six entity kinds to twelve, and a fifth variant, lean-80, sends the kind definitions once in the state instead of repeating them in every question. A third run, Jev against Claude Opus 5 answering the same questions with Fable 5.1 as judge, is built but blocked: see the first finding.

66d96fc5cb0dd906.label: IMF board paper
66d96fc5cb0dd906.description: A real 15-page IMF Executive Board information paper in which Germany notifies the Fund of EU sanctions regulations: dense legal citations, dates, countries and listed organisations. Nothing was tuned on it.

2b2a1f91b7230943.label: Sample newsletter
2b2a1f91b7230943.description: A 3-page fictional newsletter generated from the gold passages. The prompts were tuned on this text, so it shows the ceiling and not what to expect from a new document.

findings.title: Jev versus Opus 5 on the same questions: blocked by the Anthropic credit balance
findings.detail: The head-to-head is built: the identical pipeline, chunks and typed questions, answered by claude-opus-5 in Jev's place, with claude-fable-5-1 as the judge. The run on the IMF paper stopped when the Anthropic API began returning "Your credit balance is too low". Jev's three repetitions finished and Fable graded them, but every Opus call failed, so there is no comparison on this document yet. Nothing on this page comes from that Opus run. Once credit is added, one command repeats it: nerjev bench --docs out/docs-imf --variants lean-80,opus-lean-80 --claude-reps 1 --judge --judge-sample-every 3. Expect about $19.

findings.title: The one passage both actors did answer
findings.detail: A smoke test before the run put one 34-word gold passage through both. Opus 5 followed the question protocol without a slip (no skipped question, no option that was not offered) and found 7 of 7 entities. Jev found 6 of 7 and held the seventh for review at 0.60. Opus took 16.5 s and $0.12; Jev took 1.1 s and $0.0006. That is about 200 times the cost and 15 times the latency for one more entity, on a single passage. It is an anecdote, not a benchmark.

findings.title: A second judge agrees with the first
findings.detail: Fable 5.1 graded the same third of the IMF paper for lean-80 that Opus 5 had graded in the tables on this page, after the bracket fix listed below. Fable: 105 right, 33 wrong, 31 missed, F1 76.6%, relaxed F1 89.1%, type accuracy 99.2%. Opus: 110 right, 28 wrong, 47 missed, F1 74.6%, relaxed 90.2%. Two judges from different model tiers land within two points of each other. Fable passed its own calibration on the twelve-kind schema first: 56 of 56 verdicts agreed with the human labels on six gold passages.

findings.title: Sending the definitions once beats repeating them
findings.detail: On the IMF paper, lean-80 scores a judged entity F1 of 74.6% (110 right, 28 wrong, 47 missed) against 66.2% for resolve-80, which differs only in repeating all twelve definitions in every question. It also costs $0.055 against $0.194, takes 11.2 s against 24.5 s, and moves 5.0 MiB against 16.7 MiB. A tagged word costs 252 input tokens against 951. It wins on the newsletter too (98.7% against 92.1%) and on the gold passages (99.2% against 96.3%). Long criteria seem to distract a model that reads literally. Lean became the pipeline default after this benchmark; --no-lean restores the old behaviour.

findings.title: Twelve kinds doubled the cost of the old default
findings.detail: With six kinds the default pipeline processed this paper for $0.094 in 10.1 s, at 464 tokens per word. With twelve kinds and definitions in every question it is $0.194 and 24.5 s, at 951 tokens per word. Every kind added to the criteria is paid for once per word of the document. Lean mode removes that multiplier: at $0.055 it is cheaper with twelve kinds than the old default was with six.

findings.title: The document kind carries this paper
findings.detail: In the judged third of the paper, lean-80 accepted 86 documents and 67 were strictly right: whole citations such as "COUNCIL IMPLEMENTING REGULATION (EU) 2026/1393" and "Regulation (EC) No 2580/2001". In the first benchmark the bare "EU" inside those citations was the main source of lost recall. It is now part of the document's name, which is the correct reading.

findings.title: What is left is boundaries, not kinds
findings.detail: Type accuracy is 100% and relaxed F1, which forgives a boundary, is 90.2% against the strict 74.6%. Of the 28 wrong entities, 23 are real entities with a wrong edge: "Council Regulation (EC) No 881/2002 imposing", "Executive Board Decision No. 144" where the name continues "–(52/51)", and American-style dates still split at the comma. Five more are the bare word "Regulation" taken as a document.

findings.title: Lowering the accept threshold no longer helps
findings.detail: The first benchmark suggested accepting at 0.50 instead of 0.70. Under the new schema that finding is gone: recomputed from these verdicts, 0.50 gives F1 74.1% against 74.6% at 0.70. It was specific to "EU" sitting just under the line, and those mentions are now absorbed into document names. The default stays at 0.70. Calibration error is still high here, 0.163, against 0.018 on the newsletter.

findings.title: The kind "other" never clears the threshold
findings.detail: Twelve mentions typed "other" in the judged chunks were real entities and every one was held for review; none was accepted. Jev is unsure by construction about a kind defined as whatever the rest are not. Either give it concrete sub-kinds, such as currency and nationality, or accept that it feeds a review queue.

findings.title: Findings and recommendations need a sentence-level stage
findings.detail: They are clauses, not names, and a word-by-word tagger returns fragments. In a test passage, "tighten monetary policy" came out well, "foreign reserves remain" lost the rest of its finding, and "inflation has eased" was missed. This paper contains neither kind, so they cost tokens here and returned nothing. One Choice per sentence (finding, recommendation or neither) would fit Jev far better.

findings.title: No relations: the new kinds have none defined
findings.detail: Zero relations reached the graph from this paper. The schema's relations still describe companies and people. The natural additions are amends (document to document), concerns (document to location), issued_by (document to organization) and holds_office (person to officer). Each is a few lines in the schema file.

findings.title: The bigger schema hit the rate limit until requests were paced
findings.detail: The first attempt at this benchmark died on a 429: six 50,000-token requests in flight are past Jev's 250,000 tokens per second. A token pacer now spaces request starts, the first chunk of a run is sent alone to measure what a question costs, and a failed repetition no longer ends a benchmark. This run made 3,650 Jev calls with no 429 and no failure. Pacing is part of the wall times shown, which is why they are not comparable with the first benchmark's.

findings.title: A bracketed name lost its closing bracket
findings.detail: "ISIL (Da'esh)" was extracted as "ISIL (Da'esh": brackets may now sit inside a name, and only the assembler was closing them, not the boundary stage. Fixed after this benchmark, so two of the wrong boundaries above are already gone.

findings.title: Grading still costs more than extracting
findings.detail: 142 judge calls cost $6.59, against $2.59 for all 3,650 Jev calls, with the judge grading every third chunk of one repetition per variant. More entities per chunk made each judge call dearer than in the first benchmark.

findings.title: Relations that need coreference are missed
findings.detail: The four gold relations that every variant misses depend on resolving "the carmaker" or "he" to a name. Version 1 only relates entities named in the same sentence.

caveats: The tables and charts on this page are the second benchmark, judged by claude-opus-5. The Fable 5.1 figures and the Opus-versus-Jev passage appear only in the findings, because the third run did not complete.

This benchmark is not like for like with the first one. The schema changed what counts as an entity: documents and officers now count, so the same text has more entities to find and more ways to be wrong.

The judge graded every third chunk of each document, on the first repetition of each variant. Variants with different chunk sizes were judged on different slices of the text, so a gap of a few points between them is not a finding. resolve-80 and lean-80 share their chunks, so that comparison is fair.
Judged recall and F1 are estimates: the list of missed entities is the judge's own. The judge's calibration check was run with the six-kind schema and has not been repeated with twelve.
The gold set is 13 fictional passages that the prompts were tuned against, and the sample newsletter is built from 12 of them. Their scores are development numbers, not a held-out test.
Costs use list prices as of 2026-09-19 and are computed from recorded tokens when the page is built. Latency is the final successful attempt of each call; wall time includes the pacer's waits.
